newsitem.title: USA: Warmer temperatures seen for U.S. Plains, Midwest.
newsitem.headline: Warmer temperatures seen for U.S. Plains, Midwest.

text.p: The U.S. Plains and Midwest will have a couple of days to dig out of the last week's winter storms as forecasts called for temperatures to rise to normal or a few degrees above, meteorologists said.
"It looks like we have some warm days coming up," said Joel Burgio of Weather Services Corp. "The (southern) Plains are going to be very warm and the Dakotas should be generally above freezing."
High temperatures will reach into the 60s (degrees Fahrenheit) early this week in parts of Nebraska and Kansas, said Fred Gesser, chief forecaster for Weather Express Inc.

"It should be warmer the next couple of days and dry in the Plains," Gesser said. "Then we get a Pacific storm system that comes across and favors the northern tier. Any precipitation will be in the Mississippi Valley and east.
Temperatures will moderate behind that storm system, bringing highs in the southern Plains back into the 50s F.
"There is a little bit cooler weather for the end of the week," Burgio said. Thursday, Friday and Staturday look normal to a little below normal."
The Plains should remain dry during that period but the Midwest could see rain changing to snow on Wednesday.
Burgio said medium-range forecasts were inconclusive because of a discrepancy between two forecasting models.
One computer model indicated another storm system would bring snow to the Midwest Friday and Saturday while the other indicated a cool-down but little chance of precipitation.
Gesser said long-range models indicated the Plains would remain relatively mild for the next week to 10 days but he cautioned the cold weather is not gone for good.
He said another mass of cold air was building in the Yukon and Alaska and noted those systems have typically pushed south into the United States this year.
